did_you_know.text: The messenger is described as having the Lord’s Spirit upon him because the Lord has anointed him and sent him to proclaim good news to the humble, bind up the brokenhearted, and announce freedom to captives and prisoners.
The verse places “the year of the Lord’s favor” alongside “the day of vengeance of our God,” followed by a mission to comfort all who mourn.
The comfort of Zion’s mourners is described through symbolic exchanges: beauty instead of ashes, the oil of joy instead of mourning, and a garment of praise instead of a spirit of despair.

Zion’s mourners will be called “oaks of righteousness” and “the planting of the Lord,” meaning they will be seen as planted by the Lord and destined to be honored for their deeds and restored condition.
The vision of redemption includes rebuilding ancient ruins, restoring places devastated long ago, and renewing cities that have lain desolate for generations.
According to the chapter’s description, foreigners and outsiders will care for Israel’s flocks and perform agricultural work, including farming the land and tending the vineyards.

Israel is called “priests of the Lord” and “ministers of our God,” emphasizing a status of religious service and mission; it is then said that they will enjoy the wealth of the nations and boast in their riches.
Instead of shame and disgrace, Israel is promised a double portion, a double inheritance in the land, and everlasting joy.
The Lord declares that he loves justice and hates robbery, and promises to repay them faithfully and make an everlasting covenant with his people.
The joy of salvation is described through clothing: garments of salvation and a robe of righteousness, like a bridegroom adorned with a headdress and a bride decorated with her jewels.
